text: These are the ordinances you are to set before them:
When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go free without payment.
If he came alone, he shall go out alone; if he was married, his wife shall go out with him.
If his master gave him a wife and she bore him sons or daughters, the wife and her children belong to her master, and he shall go out alone.
But if the slave declares, "I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go free,"

then his master shall bring him before God.[^1]

[^1]: Or 'before the judges'; the Hebrew word can refer to God or to those who act as judges on his behalf.

versions.text: then his master shall bring him before God. He shall bring him to the door or the doorpost and pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall be his slave for life.
versions.explanation: A brief footnote helps oral readers understand the legal setting of this phrase, which is widely understood either as a sanctuary procedure before God or as an appearance before judges.

text: When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go free as male slaves do.
If she does not please the master who designated her for himself, he shall let her be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.
If he designates her for his son, he shall treat her according to the rights of daughters.
If he takes another wife, he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of the first.
And if he does not provide these three things for her, she shall go free without payment.
Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death.
But if he did not lie in wait, and God let it happen by his hand, then I will appoint a place where he may flee.
But if a man schemes against his neighbor to kill him by treachery, you shall take him even from my altar to be put to death.

versions.text: But if a man acts deliberately, killing his neighbor by treachery, you shall take him even from my altar to be put to death.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew יָזִד עַל־רֵעֵהוּ means to act presumptuously/plot against one's neighbor; the current rendering detaches the object from the verb and reads awkwardly. The infinitive לְהָרְגוֹ expresses purpose ('to kill him'), not a completed act.

text: Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
Whoever kidnaps a man—whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession—shall surely be put to death.
Whoever curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
If men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist, and the man does not die but is confined to bed,
then if he gets up and walks outside with his staff, the one who struck him is not to be punished. He must only pay for his lost time and see that he is fully healed.
If a man beats his male or female slave with a rod and the slave dies at his hand, he shall surely be punished.

versions.text: If a man beats his male or female slave with a rod and the slave dies at his hand, he shall be punished.
versions.explanation: The infinitive absolute construction נָקֹם יִנָּקֵם carries emphasis, rendered elsewhere in this chapter as 'shall surely be put to death' (vv. 12, 15, 16, 17). Adding 'surely' keeps the emphatic force and internal consistency.

text: But if the slave survives a day or two, the owner is not to be punished, for the slave is his property.

versions.text: But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be punished, for the slave was his property.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew is a nominal clause in the present ('he is his property'), stating the legal ground; the past tense 'was' is inconsistent with the present-tense legal framing of the rest of the verse.

versions.text: But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be punished, for the slave is his property.
versions.explanation: In oral reading the pronoun 'he' in 'he is not to be punished' can be heard as referring back to the slave, the nearest antecedent, whereas the Hebrew subject of לֹא יֻקַּם is the master. Naming the owner removes the ambiguity without adding content, since the master is the acting subject carried over from the preceding law.

text: If men are fighting and they strike a pregnant woman so that she gives birth prematurely, but there is no serious injury, the offender shall be fined whatever the woman's husband demands and the judges allow.
But if there is serious injury, you shall give life for life,
eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.
If a man strikes the eye of his male or female slave and destroys it, he shall set the slave free in compensation for the eye.
And if he knocks out the tooth of his male or female slave, he shall set the slave free in compensation for the tooth.
If an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox is not liable.

But if the ox has been in the habit of goring and its owner has been warned yet did not keep it penned up, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner also shall be put to death.
If a ransom is imposed on him, he shall pay whatever is imposed to redeem his life.
If the ox gores a son or a daughter, the same rule applies.
If the ox gores a male or female slave, the owner shall pay thirty shekels of silver to the slave's master, and the ox shall be stoned.
If a man opens a pit, or digs one and fails to cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit shall make restitution; he shall pay the animal's owner in silver, and the dead animal shall be his.
If one man's ox injures another's so that it dies, they shall sell the live ox and divide the money, and they shall also divide the dead animal.
But if it was known that the ox had been in the habit of goring and its owner did not keep it penned up, he must make restitution, ox for ox, and the dead animal shall be his.
If a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he shall repay five head of cattle for the ox and four sheep for the sheep.
